subsection: 6. Electoral reform, sectarianism in politics, Fenianism and Liberal reforms, 1850–1870

notes.b: The vote widened and narrowed in successive reforms, and the Irish electorate was reshaped by the 1829 and 1850 changes.
points: The Catholic Relief Act of 1829 abolished the forty-shilling freehold vote and raised the county franchise to £10, which sharply reduced the Irish county electorate.
The Reform Act of 1832 extended the vote in the boroughs and in the counties for certain occupiers, but the Irish electorate remained small by British standards.
The Irish Franchise Act of 1850 changed the qualifications for the vote in the boroughs and counties, and it reduced the number of voters in many towns.
Electoral registration and the cost of voting in public meant that landlords and the clergy could influence the votes of tenants and poorer electors.
The Irish electorate grew more slowly than the population after the Famine, and the size of the vote in many constituencies fell in the 1850s.

notes.b: Religious rivalry shaped Irish politics in the 1840s and 1850s, dividing Catholic and Protestant voters and tenant-right campaigners.
points: The Orange Order, founded in 1795, was the leading Protestant organisation and opposed Catholic claims through public demonstrations and parades.
The Dolly's Brae affair of July 1849 saw a clash between Orange and Catholic processions near Castlewellan in County Down, in which several people were killed.
The Ecclesiastical Titles Act of 1851 forbade Catholic bishops from using titles connected with English places, and it provoked widespread Catholic protest.
The Tenant League, founded in 1850, sought tenant right and the protection of tenants from eviction, and it won a number of Catholic and Presbyterian seats in 1852.
The Independent Irish Party, formed in 1852 by Catholic and Liberal MPs, aimed to secure tenant right and independence from British party politics.
The Sadleir and Keogh betrayal in the mid-1850s saw John Sadleir and John Keogh, two Irish MPs, accept government office and withdraw from the independent opposition, which wrecked the party.

notes.h: The Fenian movement: origins and organisation
notes.b: The Fenian movement was a secret revolutionary organisation that aimed to establish an Irish republic by force, drawing support from Ireland and the United States.
points: The Irish Republican Brotherhood was founded in Dublin in 1858 by James Stephens and John O'Mahony, and it became the Irish branch of the movement.
The Fenian Brotherhood was founded in New York in 1858, drawing on Irish emigrants and veterans of the American Civil War.
The name Fenian came from the Fianna, the legendary warrior band of Irish mythology, and the movement took the name to emphasise its link with Irish tradition.
The Fenians were organised in secret cells and drew support from skilled workers, shopkeepers, and young men in the towns, as well as from emigrants.
The Irish People, a newspaper founded in Dublin in 1863 and edited by Charles Kickham and others, carried the Fenian message to a wide readership.

notes.h: The Fenian rising of 1867 and its aftermath
notes.b: The 1867 rising was poorly planned and failed, but its prisoners and its executions made Fenianism a lasting political cause.
points: The Fenian rising took place in March 1867 and was crushed within days, with small risings in County Cork, County Tipperary and Dublin.
The Manchester Martyrs were three Fenians executed in Manchester in November 1867 after the killing of a police sergeant during a rescue attempt.
The Clerkenwell explosion of December 1867 in London killed several people and damaged a prison wall, provoking public anger in Britain.
Fenian raids on Canada from the United States, notably in 1866 and 1870, were intended to put pressure on Britain and were defeated.
The Church opposed Fenianism, and Archbishop Paul Cullen denounced it, which limited its support among the Catholic clergy and many farmers.
The movement's strengths were its secret organisation and its links with Irish America, and its weaknesses were poor military planning and the infiltration of its leadership by informers.

notes.b: Stephens was the founder and organiser of the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and he was a participant in the Fenian movement's early years.
points: James Stephens was born in Kilkenny in 1825, and he trained as an engineer before joining the Young Ireland and Fenian movements.
He founded the Irish Republican Brotherhood with John O'Mahony in 1858 and became its leader in Ireland, with the title of Head Centre.
He organised the Irish People newspaper and recruited large numbers of members, particularly among young men in the towns and in the army.
He was arrested in November 1865 and imprisoned in Dublin, but he escaped from Richmond Prison in November 1866.
After his escape he went to the United States, where his leadership was challenged, and the 1867 rising went ahead under the control of others.
Contemporaries regarded him as a skilled organiser but a poor military leader, and his leadership was criticised by his followers after 1867.
Historians have judged him as the founder of the modern revolutionary movement, but have noted that his organisation was too loose and that informers damaged it.

notes.b: Kickham was a writer and Fenian leader whose newspaper and novels made Fenianism a cultural as well as a political movement.
points: Charles Joseph Kickham was born in Mullinahone, County Tipperary, in 1828, and he lost most of his hearing after an accident in childhood.
He joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood and became one of its leading organisers, serving as editor of the Irish People.
He was arrested with Stephens in 1865 and imprisoned, and he was released in 1869 after a campaign for an amnesty.
His novel Knocknagow, published in 1879, depicted rural Irish life and nationalist sentiment, and it became one of the most popular Irish novels of its time.
Contemporaries admired his personal integrity and his writing, though his role in the rising was limited by his imprisonment.
Later historians have judged him as one of the most important writers and organisers of the Fenian movement, and as a figure who linked literature to politics.

notes.h: Liberal reforms: Gladstone and the Church and Land Acts
notes.b: Gladstone's first government addressed the Irish Church and land questions after 1868, in response to the Fenian threat and to tenant grievances.
points: William Ewart Gladstone became prime minister in December 1868 and promised to address the Irish question, having declared that the Irish Church needed to be disestablished.
The Irish Church Act of 1869 disestablished the Church of Ireland from 1 January 1871, ended its status as the state church, and redistributed some of its property.
The Irish Land Act of 1870 gave tenants some compensation for improvements made to their holdings and for eviction without good cause, but it did not give them full security of tenure.
The 1870 Act was limited because it did not give tenants fixed rents and left the power of landlords to evict in place, provided that compensation was paid.
The Irish University Act of 1873 was a later reform, but the 1870 measures were the main Liberal response in the period covered here.

notes.b: Judgements of the period turn on whether Fenianism or Liberal reform did more to change Irish politics by 1870.
points: Achievement of Fenianism: it kept the goal of an Irish republic alive and organised a revolutionary movement across Ireland and the United States.
Limit of Fenianism: the 1867 rising failed, and its leadership was poorly organised and frequently infiltrated by informers.
Contemporary view: the Fenians were seen by many in Britain as a dangerous conspiracy, while Irish nationalists saw them as heroic and principled.
Later view: historians have argued that Fenianism pushed Gladstone to address the Church and land questions, and that Liberal reform took much of the energy out of the movement.
Achievement of Liberal reform: the Church Act ended the established Church and the Land Act recognised tenant claims for compensation.
Limit of Liberal reform: neither measure addressed the core demands of tenant right or the political claims for Home Rule.

keyTerms.definition: The revolutionary movement, organised through the Irish Republican Brotherhood in Ireland and the Fenian Brotherhood in the United States, which aimed to establish an Irish republic by force.
The belief that Irish independence could be won only by armed rebellion, which the Fenians adopted from 1858 onwards.
Hostility and rivalry between Catholics and Protestants, which shaped electoral politics, public processions and violent clashes in the period.
The secret revolutionary organisation founded in Dublin in 1858 by James Stephens and John O'Mahony, which led the Fenian movement in Ireland.
Three Fenians executed in Manchester in November 1867 after the killing of a police sergeant during the rescue of prisoners.
The tenant-right organisation founded in 1850 that sought protection for tenants against eviction and won seats at the 1852 election.
The ending of the Church of Ireland's status as the established church, carried out by the Irish Church Act of 1869 with effect from 1871.
